hints: Think about why CFCs can survive all the way up to the stratosphere unchanged, what does that tell you about their reactivity down below?
Compare bond strengths, the $\text{C-F}$ bond is one of the strongest single bonds while $\text{C-Cl}$ is much weaker and broken by UV.
Link the weak bond breaking to Cl radicals and ozone destruction, then pick the combination with only the two true statements.
walkthrough:
**Check statement 3 - inertness**

CFCs were used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants precisely because they are very unreactive. They do not react in the lower atmosphere, so they drift unchanged up to the stratosphere.

Think: relatively inert in the troposphere = statement 3 is true.

**Check statement 1 - which bond breaks?**

In the stratosphere, high energy UV provides enough energy for homolytic fission, but only for the weaker bond.

$$\text{CCl}_2\text{F}_2 \xrightarrow{UV} \text{ }\dot{\text{C}}\text{ClF}_2 + \text{Cl}\cdot$$

The $\text{C-Cl}$ bond breaks to give a chlorine radical. The $\text{C-F}$ bond is far too strong (about 467 kJ mol-1) to be broken by this UV, so statement 1 is false.

**Check statement 2 - ozone depletion**

That $\text{Cl}\cdot$ radical then catalyses the breakdown of ozone, and is regenerated, so one Cl can destroy thousands of $\text{O}_3$ molecules.

$$\text{Cl}\cdot + \text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{ClO}\cdot + \text{O}_2$$

This catalytic cycle is the cause of the ozone hole, so statement 2 is true. True statements are 2 and 3 only.

options.A: Incorrect, as this would mean 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. Statement 1 is false because only the weaker $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is dissociated by UV, the $\text{C-F}$ bond is too strong to break.
options.B: Incorrect, as this would mean 1 and 2 only are correct. It correctly includes ozone depletion but wrongly includes statement 1 and wrongly leaves out the true inertness in statement 3.
options.C: Correct, as statements 2 and 3 only are true. CFCs are relatively inert in the troposphere which lets them reach the stratosphere, where UV breaks $\text{C-Cl}$ (not $\text{C-F}$) to release $\text{Cl}\cdot$ radicals that catalytically destroy ozone.
options.D: Incorrect, as this would mean 1 only is correct. Statement 1 is the false one, while statements 2 and 3 are both well established facts about CFCs.
